blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR DAVID HARKNESS (recalled)
Examination-in-chief by MR ASTBURY
Dr Harkness, you've given evidence in these proceedings before. I'm afraid I can't remember whether you took the affirmation or the oath.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Anyway, you are subject to --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: You are still bound to that undertaking that you took.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: You were, we know, employed at the Countess of Chester Hospital as a paediatric registrar in the summer of 2015. And you've come along today to answer questions about a shift, the night of the shift that you completed, between the 3rd and 4 August of 2015 —
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: -- and in particular, a baby by the name of [Baby E] and your dealings with [Baby E].
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: What time would your night shift have started on that occasion?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think we started at 8.30, if I remember rightly, with a half-hour handover period. It might have been 9 o'clock, I can't remember. With working in so many hospitals, it's different in every place.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So either 8.30 or 9, the shift would have started?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Would have then been followed by a handover?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: We've heard something about nursing handovers and effectively the shift finishing and the shift starting, exchanging information about the babies in their care.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Same sort of thing with the doctors?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And just very quickly, how would that take place?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So we would sit in a room together, the day team and the night team, we would have handover sheet, which would have all of the details of the patients summarised, what their diagnosis was, how old they were, if they had any outstanding issues. And we would -- the day team would go through each individual patient and tell us what had happened with them through the day.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Would that be for an individual unit?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: There would be one handover for the children's ward, one handover for the neonatal unit, but the same doctors would be in both.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Okay. So you'd be assuming responsibility for both units on nights?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And anywhere else, should you be needed?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: A&E. If there were any sick children, then we would attend A&E as well.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: How long typically would that handover take?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Typically, you expect it to be 30 minutes. It can be longer, but typically a 30-minute handover.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So that would have finished either at 9 or 9.30 depending on when the shift began or thereabouts?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Where would that handover have taken place?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That happens on the children's ward.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Okay. Do you recall who you were working with that night on the shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: From my personal recollection, no. From looking through the case notes, there was a Dr Chris Wood who was my SHO.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Would he too be required to cover both the children's and the neonatal unit on that night shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Did you work together or would you work separately?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Depends on what we were doing. Some tasks would require both of us together, other tasks we would work independently. So it very much depended on the complexity.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: The handover having finished, do you recall specifically what you'd have done next on that particular shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So not that particular shift. Typically it would be that we would look for -- if there were a sick patient, to go and review a sick patient, otherwise talk to the nurses on children's ward for any of their concerns and then go over to the neonatal unit to see if there were any concerns there. But I can't remember any specifics from that shift.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Okay. So on that typical course of events what sort of time would you expect to be going to the neonatal unit on a regular night shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Very much depending on what was happening elsewhere.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Typically, if there was nothing on the children's ward, I'd expect to be there by 10/10.30.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Okay. Do you recall on that particular shift what time you went over to the neonatal unit?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: From my statement and the notes, it was approximately 10 o'clock, 10 pm.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: That's based on the notes that you've seen?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And did the notes explain to you why you attended, if there was any reason in particular?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I was called to see [Baby E], who had had some blood in some vomit and blood up his NG tube, the tube that goes into his stomach.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Do you recall whether you were shown anything when you arrived?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I was shown a sample of this, what we call a bloody aspirate or a dirty aspirate, which was essentially stomach contents that was pulled back up through the tube, that had some small amounts of blood in it.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Could you expand a little bit on small amounts of blood?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think what I've put is flecks and what I remember is flecks, so it'd be tiny, minuscule amounts of blood, so no large clots, no fresh blood, it would be tiny spots of blood throughout.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Perhaps we should go to your note for the detail of what then happened. If I can ask Mr Murphy to take us to tile 128 and the notes behind, please. If we scroll down.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Your name at the top, you recognise the handwriting?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Your handwriting?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Cast your eye over the note. That's only half of the note, I think it follows on to the next page, but if it just helps you refresh your memory for a moment. Then I'll ask you to take us through it.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I have put:
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "Asked to see re gastric bleed. Large, very slightly bilestrained aspirate 30 minutes ago."
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Pausing there. The time on the left-hand side of the page, what does that represent, the time you arrived, the time you made the note? Are you able to --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That would be the time that I've written the note.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Right. When you talk about "30 minutes ago", are you able to tell us roughly what time now that would have been?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Based on that, that would be between 9.30 and 9.45 would have been what I'd expect from that -- where I would have been, sorry? If I'd not been at that point on the unit, then I would have been on the children's ward.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And the reference to 30 minutes, was that what you knew to be the case or what you were being told by --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: What I'd been told.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: -- whoever was passing the information on? When you arrived at the NNU, did you go straight to [Baby E] as a result of the request?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And who was there when you arrived?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Nurse Letby was there. I can't remember who else was in the room at the time.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Sorry, the next line, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Sudden large vomit of fresh blood and 14ml aspirate."
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Pausing there, is that something you were told or something that you saw?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: This is something that I've seen.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Just tell us then, please, you've arrived to meet Ms Letby and [Baby E] in -- do you remember which nursery they were in?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Nursery 1.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: You're told that there's been a large, very slightly bile-stained aspirate 30 minutes ago, and you are shown an aspirate?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. So what I'm shown at this point has got the small amounts of fresh blood and a total of 14ml, which would have been sucked up through the NG tube into a syringe.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So 14ml and there was blood in that.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Are you able to help with what the 14ml comprised?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That was mostly stomach contents, so I can't remember exactly, but it would have been a combination of stomach acid and milk.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: How did this note then -- or what developed to give cause to this note:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Sudden large vomit of fresh blood"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Could you rephrase that, sorry?
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: What gave rise to this entry?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: This would be when I was called to review, so I would have reviewed at this time, being called to look at this vomit, and then made this recording of my decision at the time.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So, "Sudden large vomit of fresh blood" -- sorry, my understanding was that you were there when this happened.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So I was called for the large vomit which had a small amount of blood in it. The fresh blood came later.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Right. So when did that come?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't remember the exact times. It should be documented in my notes, I think. I can't remember what I've put in my statement for the exact timing but that was within the next following hour to 2 hours.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Just concentrating on this note for now, this second line, "Sudden large vomit of fresh blood", when did that happen?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So I think... I don't think I was referring there for the large amounts of fresh blood. I think I'm commenting on large vomit with blood and 14ml of aspirate. So I don't think expressly that's me saying that there is large amounts of blood for this initial review, I would need to see the rest of my note.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: All right. If we scan to the next page, please, just so you can finish reading it in full.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So this was the small amount of blood in this one, looking at what I've written there. So I've reviewed the observations on the previous page, I have examined [Baby E], and I've put -- the triangle there is my suspicion of diagnosis of GI bleeds, query cause.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: I'm going to ask you to pause because I want to go through the note in order.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Certainly.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Perhaps if you look at the next entry at 11 o'clock, just to orientate yourself as to the events that follow, and we'll go back to the start of the 10.10 notes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: (Pause)
Okay.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: There is a note later (inaudible: coughing) if that helps you distinguish the first sequence of events. So you're called and at 10.10, you record that you were told there was a "large, very slightly bile-stained aspirate", 30 minutes before, presumably, your arrival.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So the "sudden large vomit of fresh blood", when was that on this occasion --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That was on this occasion when I was called.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And were you there when this took place?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't think I was there when this took place. From looking at the whole set of notes, I think I was called to see this one. For the subsequent ones I was on the unit.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: All right. It says:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Sudden large vomit of fresh blood..."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is that an and?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "... 14ml of aspirate."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So was this another aspirate or the one that you are referring to in the line above?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: This was the same -- this was part of this, this was the... Not the bile-stained one from 30 minutes ago, this was the 14ml plus a vomit that happened that I was called to see.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Right, okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm sorry, I'm probably being very stupid, but I'm not understanding this. Let's just take this in stages:
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: "Asked to see patient re gastric bleed."
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So that implies that you've been called to a patient who has had a gastric bleed.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So this was the bloodstained vomit that I was called to see. So chronologically, 30 minutes before my arrival, there was a large bile-stained vomit that I haven't seen. And then at 10.10, I've been called to see the sudden large vomit of fresh blood and 14ml of aspirate, which has happened at around about the 10 pm mark, where I've been asked to go and see. So these are separate vomits 30 minutes apart.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: But two vomits before you get into the unit?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'll return to it in questioning later. I have to say, my Lord, that is not the way I had understood it. It sounded as if there had been a visit to the unit, then gone away, and then come back for the second one but I can explore that later.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I need to see the rest of the notes to see the exact timings.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Have you seen the notes this morning?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I've seen my statement this morning.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: But you haven't seen these notes?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I've not seen the notes, no.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We'll see whether the nursing notes fit with my exact timings.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: I think you'd better go back over this and try and make it clear because at the moment, to me, it's unclear.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Is this a process to complete now with Dr Harkness?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, I think so. I think go through the notes and then invite the doctor to talk to the notes, speak to the notes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: All right.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we go then, please, down to the next page, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Take a moment, please, Dr Harkness, to look -- finish the 22.10 note and then also go on to read, please, the 23.00 note.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I've put on examination --
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Sorry, could you --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Read it to yourself first of all.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Refresh your memory and get the chronology in your head and we'll go back to the start.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: So to look at the exact timings of the first one, I would need to see the nursing notes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: We can do that as well. If we have a look at your notes first --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Certainly from this point of view...
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: -- then we'll go to the nursing notes --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, all right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: If we can scroll up, you can have a look at your 23.00 hours note, please.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: (Pause).
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: If I can ask Mr Murphy please, next, to go to tile 149.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: (Pause)
Okay.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: (Pause)
Then if we go, I think, to tile 127. Go to the nursing notes behind, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: (Pause)
We can make it a little larger for you, it'll be easier to read.
I think it'll be the previous one.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: If we go to the previous tile, please. Sorry, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The bottom right, thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: (Pause)
Okay, that makes it clearer.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Again, just so we perhaps don't need to come back to this, if you look at the next note as well, please, if we go back to 127.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: (Pause)
Okay.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Right. If we come out of the nursing notes, please, and just for the sake of completeness, I'm going to ask Mr Murphy next to go to tile 160 and look at the notes behind.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not your handwriting, Dr Harkness, but I don't think there's any dispute you were present at 01.30; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: If you just want to refresh your memory too from those events.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: (Pause)
Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So if we go back to 128, please, and the notes behind.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Hopefully that's refreshed your memory of the whole of the relevant sequence on that shift.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Apologies for that. If we look now at "Sudden large vomit of fresh blood and 14ml aspirate", does that fit that entry into the chronology as you now recall?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that would have been some fresh blood and 14ml taken from the tube. It's not clear from what I've written how much of that 14ml was fresh blood versus mixed with stomach contents, and I don't know how much of that was fresh -- was all fresh blood. However, that was the first instance of blood, fresh blood, seen. So the flecks were something -- I think what I've put there is bile-stained, I think... I've seen the bilestained aspirate when I've come, and then I've seen the fresh blood on my arrival.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sorry for the confusion.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: No, no.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, can we just then be clear? What you've written down here, how much of that was what you were told or how much of that was you actually witnessed?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The blood is what I've witnessed. This is what I've seen. The bile-stained is something that I've been told, possibly seen. The blood I have definitely seen, that's something that I've been called over to see and I have seen for myself definitely.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Have you seen it actually occurring or have you just seen the product?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I have been called for the product --
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: To see the product?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: This was the product, sorry.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Sorry, as I said, it was me being stupid.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I think that makes it clearer.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It's so long ago, it's difficult.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Of course it is and you're reliant on your notes largely.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I think, I'll be corrected if I'm wrong, you were told about the bile flecks, you arrived, you think it was that second entry that caused you to be called?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And you were shown that product?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: All right. The next line, "Background". Could you read your entries there?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Reduced end-diastolic flow."
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: That's the flow of blood from the placenta into baby. When they do an ultrasound in the womb they will look to see the blood flow and there will be less blood flow than you would like to see. What this means in respect of this is that it can increase the risk of a lack of blood to the bowel and problems with the bowel. I've put IUGR, which is intrauterine growth restriction. So that's a small baby, smaller that you'd expect the baby to be at that point in time.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: I have put:
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "Re-screened for increased oxygen requirement yesterday and a CRP of less than 1."
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So his oxygen had gone up for the previous day, or the previous team, due to his oxygen going up, and so he was restarted on antibiotics. Bloods sent to look for bacteria in the blood and the CRP being a sign of infection, which was less than 1, which doesn't suggest there being any infection at that point in time.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Pausing there, you say his oxygen went up; is that his oxygen requirement?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Oxygen requirement, yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And then I've put "opening bowels". So that was important in that if babies have problems with their bowels, their bowels tend to go to sleep and they tend to stop passing poo.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So that's why you have recorded that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's why I've recorded that, yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: There are some figures recorded thereafter. Could you take us through those?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I have put:
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "Mean blood pressure of 48."
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Ideally at his age you'd want that above 30, so you've got your top blood pressure, your bottom blood pressure, and we are more interested in something that comes in between. So 48 was very good at that point in time and nothing of concern.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: CRT, which is cap refill time, of less than 2, which is ideal, that's where we want it.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Heart rate I've put of 140 to 100. I don't know why I put it that way round. But essentially, that's the normal rate. 100 to 140, I'd be very happy with that for a baby.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Saturations of 100% in 23% oxygen, FiO2. So again his oxygen level now is very minimal, he's breathing well for himself, the saturations can only go as high as 100, we tend to want them in the 90s. So at that point in time everything is fine other than the blood that I have seen.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Right. If we scroll down to the next page, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "OE"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: OE is on examination. So I put that he's alert, pink, well perfused, so nice and pink throughout his limbs.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Cap refill time less than 2. Heart rate was normal.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: The diagram is a picture of his lungs. A cross through the lungs essentially means that the lung fields are clear, so I can't hear any suggestion of reduced air entry onto the lungs or any crackles or signs of infection.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: I have put:
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "Abdo soft, not distended. BS [bowel] sounds +."
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So at this point his bowels are still moving away, I can hear that they have not gone to sleep, they're still working.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: His tummy is nice and soft and not distended. If a child has problems with their bowels or their stomach you tend to find the stomach expands, the abdomen tends to expand with it as well. In this case that was all normal.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: I have put "AF normotensive". The AF is the anterior fontanelle, the soft spot on the front of the head. Normotensive just means it's normal.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "Femorals ++", so we feel the pulses in the groin.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And plus plus means they're both present and they're both strong enough for me to feel them, which is good.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: I have put the diagnosis:
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "GI bleed, [query] cause."
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Let's pause. Just take a break and ease down a little bit and slow it down, I hope. The little triangle that you have drawn, is that code for something?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That is a delta sign, we tend to put that for diagnosis.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: You put GI bleed? Just explain that to us, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's gastrointestinal bleed, so blood has come from somewhere between the oesophagus and the anus, that's the GI tract.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And that's based on what you have seen?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's based on me seeing blood that's come into the tube and has been vomited.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And you're querying the cause. Presumably that's what then informs your plan that follows?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Take us through the plan.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I have put:
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "IV [so intravenous] ranitidine."
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Ranitidine is a medication that reduces the acid produced by the stomach, so if you've got increased acid or irritation to the stomach, it can help to reduce that. So we'll tend to give that if there's any suspicion of any blood.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: I have put, "Add metronidazole". Metronidazole is a different type of antibiotic we use to cover for necrotising enterocolitis, so I've put in brackets:
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "At risk of NEC."
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Pausing there. You mentioned earlier that that's something that arises out of absent end-diastolic flow; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's something that comes with prematurity. A risk factor for that will be being small and having that reduction of the blood flow through the placenta.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So that was a possibility that was in your mind?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It was on my mind. It wasn't fitting with it at this point in time. There was nothing else to suggest it.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: However, because of the vomit, and because of that background, that was where my decision came to add the antibiotic.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: The next entry, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's "close observation" because, obviously, I'm concerned at this point and I want to make sure he continues to be closely supervised. He was in room 1, so he would have been at the highest level of care anyway. It's just to reiterate the point.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Just pausing there, who would be responsible for close observation?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That would have been the nurse looking after him, who was Nurse Letby.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Okay. Next one, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I have put:
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "Repeat FBC [for full blood count] mane [morning]."
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Essentially, if you have had any blood loss, if you do a blood test straight away, you don't tend to notice any difference because your body is yet to compensate.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: When you check it the following morning, if there is a significant amount of blood that's been lost, you'll notice that that result drops. And then you could make further treatment, such as giving blood, based on that.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Right. And the last line, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I put:
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "Discussed with [Dr C], happy with plan."
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So that was a telephone conversation.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And we've heard that [Dr C] was the consultant on call --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: -- at that stage?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So at 11 o'clock, we have your next entry. Can you recall what you did after your examination of [Baby E]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Following my previous -- I can't tell from that point of view whether I left the unit or whether I stayed on the unit based on that entry. I think from my recollection, I certainly didn't go very far away because this was something that was unusual -- and the time frame would suggest that I wasn't very far away either. But I don't think I left the unit.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: As a matter of interest, you told us you started on the children's ward --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: -- and then you made your way to the neonatal ward.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: How far is that, how long would that take ordinarily?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: A couple of minutes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Having refreshed your memory from your notes and the entirety of the shift, tell us, please, what you recall from 11 o'clock.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So from 11 o'clock, from what I remember happening -was suddenly a large amount of fresh blood being seen in the tube.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Pausing there, by you or you were alerted to that by others?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't remember whether I was -- from what I remember I was on the unit and I was called to come into the room to see it, so I had seen it as it happened.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Do you remember who called you into the room?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Nurse Letby.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Then, from what I remember, from that point of view, he'd suddenly then deteriorated following that and needed ventilating, which then continued to deteriorate, needed bloods -- needed medications to give his blood pressure up, needed fluids to try and help expand the amount of blood going around the body, and then sadly continued to deteriorate and passed away.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Let's go through it step-by-step, if we may, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's probably a summary of --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: -- what remained of the shift. Can we start with 11 o'clock?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: 11 o'clock.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: You've got the blood loss and a desaturation -- is that to 70%?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So 70% -- so further blood coming through the tube and I remember seeing this in the tube at this time, seeing at this point fresh red blood in the tube.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: If we go to the next line:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "13ml bloodstained fluid."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is that what you're talking about?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. So this was fresh blood in with a bit of stomach content and then -- that's from the NG on free drainage.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: The NGT is the tube going into the nose. Free drainage is essentially -- normally you put a little bung on the end of the tube to stop anything from coming up. If you're worried that a baby is vomiting, the last thing we want is that vomit to get on to the lungs, so by putting a syringe on to the end of it what happens is that anything will come up with that tube with the pressure and go into this little syringe instead. So free drainage is what that means. So everything should come up into that tube, so the whole stomach contents should come up.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Is that how you're able to tell us the volume of what —
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. So this is within the tube -- if it was vomit you obviously can't tell because it's everywhere, but this was bloody fluid that was in the actual tube, it came up the tube into this syringe at the end, so we can measure that.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: The fact that it's coming up the tube, does that assist with perhaps where its origin is?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. So because it's come up that tube, it has to have come from somewhere along the gastrointestinal tract.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So it could have been the oesophagus that's been swallowed into the stomach and come up through the stomach, it could have been within the stomach itself.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: What this rules out this being is any blood that's come from the lungs because any blood that had coughed up from the lungs wouldn't have come into the tube, it would have come out through the mouth and through the nose.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Right. We've got some more entries on the next page.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I have put:
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "BP [so blood pressure] stable."
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: His mean blood pressure was still good at 43. His heart rate at this point had gone up slightly from 140 to 160, previously it was 100 to 140, still not high enough for me to be overly concerned. His saturations, so the amount of oxygen in the blood, has dropped down to 60 to 70%, so very low. And he's now requiring 100% oxygen to keep them where they are. But I have put he's making good respiratory effort, so he's still breathing for himself, and crying.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Can we pause there and just consider that entry, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Certainly.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So at some point, you told us earlier he was in oxygen at about 23%?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: At some point because of his condition that's had to be increased?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And despite that, his saturations are dropping as low as 60 to 70%?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: How does that fit in with the fact that he's making a good respiratory effort?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So he's still trying to breathe at this point in time.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So what can happen is a baby can either stop breathing and they will drop or they'll not be breathing fast enough to get the oxygen in or, in his case, he was still breathing, taking big breaths to try and get the oxygen in the blood, but something at this point in time is interfering with how that oxygen is getting into his bloodstream.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Right. And you comment on him crying. Is that of relevance?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So at this point he's well enough at this point in time, he's still able to cry, he's still awake, he's still crying, he's not unconscious. I have not commented on what kind of cry this is, but from looking at the rest of my documentation at this point in time it suggests he's still well enough to be able to cry, as a baby would. If I put just as crying it would be a typical cry that I would expect from -- any baby to make.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Does the ability to cry tell you anything about the oxygen or the air going in and out of the chest?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: You have to be able to take -- as anyone with a baby knows, babies have to be able to take a big breath in to be able to make the noise when they cry. You need to push that air out, same with talking. You have to be able to get air into your lungs to get it out. You have to be awake enough to be able to coordinate crying and your brain to tell you to want to cry. So at this point he is still awake and he is still taking big breaths to be able to cry.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Right. So based on the situation at 11 o'clock and that second loss of blood, you draft a plan again. Could you take us through that, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I have put:
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "Replace losses with 20ml per kg of 0.9% saline."
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So essentially what we'll do at this point in time is because we're measuring how much is coming out, we can then replace that with giving fluid back in again. So what I have done is given him salt water -- the first thing you would do is give some salt water rather than blood because it's much quicker to get into the system and order because we have it there.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: I have put "strict fluid balance". I want to make sure I know exactly how much is coming out so I know exactly how much to put back in and also as part of that how much he's weeing, which can be a sign of how sick he is.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: I have put:
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "For elective intubation with drugs."
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So that's me putting the tube into his lungs to breathe for him. Although he's breathing for himself, because he needs so much oxygen, I want to make sure I can help him as much as possible and give him rest.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So I am going to intubate him at this point in time, I have also planned to do a chest X-ray -- CXR is chest X-ray, AXR is abdominal X-ray -- to look to see if there's anything that changed on his lungs, to look to see why his oxygen's gone up and also to see if anything's happening within his abdomen that would suggest why he is deteriorating well and why he is bleeding.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Just going back to the entry concerning intubation, it's described as an elective intubation.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So at this point he's well enough -- elective would mean I've got enough time to plan it and give medication.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: You have elective and emergency. At this point he's well enough for me to give him medications to sedate him and give him some muscle relaxants to make it much easier to intubate him and make it much more pleasant for the baby when they're going through the experience as well. So it's a much more controlled environment to do this at this point in time.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Right. There is presumably another type of intubation?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The opposite would be an emergency intubation where you have no time to give medications and you just have to go as fast as you can, essentially, to get the tube into the lungs.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: We may come back to that in a moment. But at this stage elective intubation --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: -- time to do it, with drugs.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: -- and not what you describe as an emergency intubation?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Okay. I think we've got "discussed with surgeons", is that, the next line?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. That's "Discuss with surgeons with X-ray results".
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So once I would have the X-ray, if there was anything suspicious to go with the cause of the bleeding, I would then call the surgical team in Alder Hey to discuss with them what I found and any suggestions they would have and then I've put:
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "[Dr C] updated, happy with plan."
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: As far as getting the X-rays and discussing them with the surgeons, what sort of timescale would you expect for that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: X-rays at night, you tend to be looking at, at best, 15 minutes, typically 30 minutes. They have one radiologist covering the entire hospital, so the timing very much depends on if there's other sick patients within the hospital, if there's someone in A&E that's very sick that needs an X-ray. Because the X-ray needs to come to the neonatal unit as opposed to the baby going to them, it's a much more time-consuming process, but I would expect 15 to 30 minutes as an average.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Again, you just made the point, you discussed it with [Dr C] and she has nothing to add to that plan?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Okay. So do you recall what you did next after that particular set of observations and conversation with [Dr C]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: At that point I have made the plan to intubate, I would have prescribed the medications and I would have been getting ready to intubate, so I would have been getting -- the
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: nurses would be getting the drugs ready, I would be preparing my equipment to plan to intubate the baby.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: With that in mind and pausing there, let me get the right reference, please, given its importance.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: (Pause)
J2645, please. It may be that we can enlarge those a little bit.
We can see a prescription, do you agree, for the pharmacy?
Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: We can see the name of the drugs, atropine sulphate, injection, the size of the dose, and the timing of that particular prescription at 23.28.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we scroll down to the activity, it was a little bit higher than I was going to draw that attention to, but while we're on that we can see it wasn't actually given because on the right we've got "Filed at 04.58"; do you agree?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: If we can go to the top half again, please, just to confirm the doctor who wrote the prescription. We have "New order by ST.WOCH". Knowing how these codes tend to be made, are you able to help us with which doctor wrote the prescription?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I would make the assumption that that's Chris Wood based on the letters involved. Yes, it's normally surname followed by first name, first and last digits -- first digits.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: If we go back to the whole (inaudible: coughing) and just scroll through it, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's the atropine sulphate. If we go to the next, please, the next prescription. 2647 for the next one.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sorry, can you say that again?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: 2647 for the next prescription.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's for morphine sulphate?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Another preparatory drug for intubation?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Thank you. If we go to the next prescription, please, which is 2647. I think the number's now obscured by an enlargement. Not a complaint. 2649, thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Possibly the page before. There's three prescriptions in the file.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's the right page. Give us the title of that drug.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Suxamethonium chloride.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Thank you. Again, another preparatory drug for intubation?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, it's a muscle relaxant.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So plan drafted at 11 o'clock. Prescriptions being written and prepared possibly at 23.28. I'll take you to your next entry, please, which you've refreshed your memory from already and that is at tile 149, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So written at 01.45, doctor. Do you recognise this note?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And you explain:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Sudden deterioration at 23.40."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So this is around 40 minutes later. Do you remember where you were when this --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I was still on the unit. I was getting ready to intubate electively and having everything ready, before this suddenly happening as I was there.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Do you know how you were alerted to it?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I was in the room when this happened.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Right. Anyone else in the room at the time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Nurse Letby was there. I believe there was another nurse there because they were together making up the drugs to be given for the elective intubation. I can't remember who else was in the room at that time.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And then talk us through, please, your observations to the right-hand side of that page.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I have put:
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "Bradycardia [which is slow heart rate] of 80 to 90 beats per minute."
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: We want that to be above 100, so when it goes below 100 we start to be concerned:
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "Saturations of 60%. Poor perfusion."
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So there's -- now the fingers and toes and the arms and legs, the blood supply is more sluggish:
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "Colour change over the abdomen with these purple discoloured patches."
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Would you like me to go into that more?
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: In a moment. Just before we do that, between 23.00 and 23.40, we saw in your earlier entry that the baby was to be placed under close observations. Did that change over that period?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, he'd still be under close observation in the room.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And again would that be his designated nurse?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: The type of observations, presumably, would include all the type of figures that you've quoted, saturations --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: -- heart rate, all that sort of information --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: -- on the monitors for the nurse to monitor --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: -- throughout?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Describe to us, please, the colour change over the abdomen that you describe in your notes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So this was a strange pattern over the tummy area, over the abdomen, which didn't fit with the poor perfusion.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: In between the kind of chest, upper legs, the rest was still pink, but there were these kind of strange purple patches that appeared over the outside of his tummy.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Pausing there, you are moving the palms of your hands around your abdomen to different places, as you do it.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Were they static, these patches?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: From what I remember there were patches in one area, then there were some in the other. Some of it was still nice and pink. But it certainly was unusual and not fitting with a baby that had completely shut down with its -- or poor perfusion.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Just breaking this down, perfusion was poor. How is that assessed?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's assessed by looking at the capillary refill time, but also when you look at the body, if you're looking at the arms and legs, you'll notice that rather than pink they'll be dusky, so more of a purplish colour. A different colour to this: this was kind of a purply-blue colour. The best example would be if you go for a swim in the cold and you come out and you get that blue around your lips, we would call that a dusky colour and that's what you tend to see. So this was different in colour and different in pattern to what you would see from a perfusion perspective.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Perfusion being the skin to --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The blood supply to the surface of the skin.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And when you were talking about pink a moment or two ago, tell us what was pink.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: His head was pink, his upper legs, upper arms, chest was pink. The abdomen was purple. Purple patches.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: A pink colour you'd expect to see?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, a normal skin colour that any well person would have.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So these purple -- how would you describe them, purple...?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So patches, so not one solid purple area. I'd say one purple patch to the bottom, one purple patch to the top.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Some in between. I can't remember exactly where they were. But they were -- where they were didn't fit with a particular
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: anatomical part of the body. It's very difficult to describe. With not having any photos or anything like that and this not being something that that I've seen.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Not seen what, you were saying?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Not seeing it outside of the babies in this case, it's difficult for me to describe it in any clearer details.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: I was about to ask you how big the patches were, but let's just deal with that point now. Had you seen it before?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'd seen this in [Baby A] and that's the only other time prior to this that I'd seen it.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Okay. Have you seen it since?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not outside of the babies in this case, no.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: This is back in 2015. Are you still practising as a paediatrician?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I'm a paediatric consultant now.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So I was going to ask you how big these patches were.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Are you able to estimate the size or were they different?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: They were different sizes, they weren't small dots, they would have been relative to the size of the baby they were in the region of 1 to 2-centimetre patches, possibly bigger, but I wouldn't say any smaller than that.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: You're moving your hands around while you're describing --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sorry.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Obviously this is being audio recorded and not video recorded. Are you moving your hands because they moved or just to indicate the different locations?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: (Indicating). The areas were over the abdomen, so not up on the chest, not below his groin, just in the middle section. From what I remember, it did change where they were, they were purple in one area and then they were purple in another, which again was strange in that you'd expect if it was something like perfusion, once your perfusion is poor to an area it tends to stay poor until you've done something to change the situation.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: I was about to ask. When you started to tell us about them, you said they didn't fit in with the perfusion you could see.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Is that what you were talking about?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: You would expect the area to stay the same if there was a problem?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. If I was to expect that his abdomen was dusky or white from perfusion, I would expect, at that point, his whole body to look the same because it tends to move -- feet and arms first, moves towards the body and the head. So to have a pink head and a pink chest, pink upper legs, and have this in the middle doesn't fit with a pattern of poor perfusion.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: It might be an obvious question, no doubt I'll be forgiven, but why does this paleness or lack of perfusion start at the ends of hands and feet?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The way our bodies work to survive is if there's something that's affecting our blood supply, we want to protect our organs and our body would rather lose arms and legs than it would lose the organs, so it protects the brain typically, the heart, to a lesser extent the kidneys, the liver, the bowels, but it will pull all of the blood in your body that it can into the middle, so the middle tends to stay pink for longer and the outside -- same as when you get cold, essentially, to heat up your body, to keep everything working, the outside gets cold and changes colour and the middle stays a better colour.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: But on this occasion it's the middle where you're seeing these discolourations?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Discolourations consistent with any symptoms that, even if you hadn't seen them, you were familiar with?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Nothing I'd seen before, no, or since.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Next line, Dr Harkness:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Intubated as an emergency at 23.45."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: You have already dealt with the distinction between elective and emergency. But why had it become an emergency?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So because we've now got this dropping in heart rate and the perfusion has started to change, the timing is a lot more imminent, but I need to get on and do this now, although it's more uncomfortable for the baby, the risk of still giving those medications and taking my time outweighs the benefits to the baby. Also, the medications that we give can also theoretically drop blood pressure, so if your blood pressure is okay but your heart rate is going fast, the last thing we would want to do is tip the balance -- sorry, if your heart rate is going slow, it will continue to go slow, not fast, and the saturation -- the heart -- blood pressure could drop. At this point the safer option is to do things as an emergency and not give the drugs.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Okay. Next line, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I have put:
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "Anterior cords, able to pass size -- unable to pass size 3 ET tube."
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: I'm going to ask you, anterior cords, what are they?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Your vocal cords sit at the top of your windpipe. Most of the time they sit nicely in the middle, so that when you go to look with a laryngoscope, they sit in a nice view and it's quite easy to pass a tube. Sometimes they can be off to the side or they can be anterior, so slightly further forward, so if they are slightly further forward it makes it more complicated to put the tube in.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So what I've done is I've gone in with a size 3, which is the width of the tube, and because of where the cords were and the view I've got, wasn't able to get that to the place that I wanted it.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Are you able to say what effect did you view?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's the anatomy, it's the way that the body -different people's bodies aren't the same. I would say anterior cords are relatively common. They do make it more difficult. There are ways and means around correcting it, with smaller tubes being the most common way to do it, which is what I've then gone on to say as I've used a size 2.5 tube, passed on my second attempt, and I've passed that 7 metres -- not metres, 7 centimetres from the lips down into the windpipe.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: I have then commented that the air entry was good and there was good chest movement. So if the air entry is -- if I can hear that there's air getting into both lungs and the chest is moving then I know that that tube is in the correct position.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: We've also got something called a capnograph, which looks at the carbon dioxide coming from the lungs. If you are breathing or you're being -- the breathing is done for you, carbon dioxide will come out of your lungs and it will change colour. So between all of those factors, I'm happy that my tube is in the correct place.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And the capnograph tells you that gases are passing in and --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Passing in and passing out, yes. It tells you that your -- you've got the gas exchange as well. So you have to have your heart beating as well as your lungs working to get the blood circulating for the carbon dioxide to come out.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Then I think you've entered the settings on the ventilator?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, at this point he's awake and this is synchronised, so this means it will try and match up with his breaths.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Pressure of 22/5, which is an average place to start.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Still needing 100% oxygen. And I put the rate of breathing at 60. So his normal breathing would be when he's well, or a baby's normally well, 30 to 40. So 60 means I'm just pushing it a little bit harder to try and get that oxygen circulating a bit better.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: We've then got an entry concerning his sats. 60 to --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is that after or before you have intubated?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: This is whilst I've intubated?
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sorry, after I've intubated they're still low.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: I have then given morphine as a bolus. So if babies are on the ventilator and they're still quite active -- and one of the benefits of the elective intubation is that the morphine will sedate them and keep them more comfortable. So what I have done
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: there is, because he's uncomfortable because of the emergency, I have given the morphine and, after having the morphine, his saturations have come up to 80%. So that suggests he is now more relaxed and more comfortable.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: There's then a comment about the purple discolouration again.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So this purple discolouration, I have put there, has remained on the abdomen, his blood -- I have then put his cuff blood pressure, so a cuff being on the arm -- we can check blood pressures centrally through putting catheters in but this will be from a blood pressure on his arm and this has now dropped to 36, which is still, for his gestation, still reasonable but starting to decrease.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So my plan at this point was to give a further fluid bolus to help with his blood pressure. I then thought about medications called inotropes. Inotropes help your heart beat stronger and they can make it beat stronger and also in combination make it beat faster. So if your blood pressure is dropping, we tend to think about these medications to get things pumping faster and stronger to help keep the blood pressure up and get the blood supply going better.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: What I then put is "could worsen bleeding". So my concern at this point in time is if I'm making the heart beat faster and stronger, is this actually going to make him bleed more rather than not. So this was me -- that was one of my thoughts at that point in time.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: I'm going to ask you to pause there because in your note of 22.10, there's a clear reference to blood, and in the note at 23.00, there's a clear reference to blood. Was there still -- was blood still a feature during the course of this episode or not?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: From my recollection, there was no further bleeding after -- at this point in time the bleeding had settled.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: There was later further bleeding. But from my recollection, I can't remember there being substantial amounts of blood at this point in time.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Your next entry, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The next entry is "[query] FFP", which is fresh frozen plasma. That contains clotting factors, so there's a possibility in small babies that they don't have the ability to clot properly and so what we do is we can replace -- between a couple of different products, we can give them more. At this point in
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: time we didn't know if there was anything wrong with his clotting, so not having anything available would mean that -unsure of the benefit. Any blood product you give comes with the risk of a reaction. So at this point it was felt that we needed those blood tests back before we gave that.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Is that the next line, which says:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Bloods sent for coagulation and cross-match"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Cross-match is what you do if you want to give -- ton find out someone's blood group. So before you give blood, what you need is to know their type. You can give universal donor blood in an emergency, but ideally you give one that is matched to the baby's blood type.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: It reduces the risk of reaction.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So at this point we've arranged for those and I've again discussed this with [Dr C], who was happy with that plan, and she was going to come across to review the patient as well.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Coagulation, so everybody understands?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sorry, that's the blood clotting. So it will look at how long it takes for your blood to clot with various sophisticated tests that they do in the lab.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Okay. We can come back to that in due course.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: My Lord, I'm conscious we started a little bit later than anticipated. I just observe it's now 12.30.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, yes. I'm becoming a little anxious now because we haven't got a full afternoon ahead of us.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm couching it as neutrally as I can.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: About how long further do you think you'll be examining Dr Harkness in chief?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Twenty minutes, I'd imagine, or so.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't know how long you're likely to be.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Maybe about an hour or so, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We're not going to finish today.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Unless we have a much shorter lunch break.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Unless you want a break now, let's try and finish the
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: examination-in-chief, get this 20 minutes done, then it's all in
one piece. And then we will see where we are.
Press on, please.
Thank you.

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.

blocks.text: Stayed throughout.

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't remember. I think we'd had a discussion for 10 or 15 minutes -- I think she was there quite quickly after I'd had that conversation with her but I can't say exactly how long that was.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "On my arrival around 00.25..."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Sorry, I thought it was up. I'm racing ahead, I do apologise.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Can we go to tile 160, thank you, and the note behind it.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: We went through it yesterday with [Dr C]. The jury will be familiar with it, but Dr Harkness can go through it.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, from Dr Harkness' perspective, of course.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I think that reflects what I've written in my entry. They're pretty much the same observations or thereabouts. The heart rate has come up above 100, so that's improved. The saturations were as I recalled and the blood pressure stayed around about the same place.

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: -- provided.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "No detectable heart rate." Was CPR commenced then?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: All right. We've heard a little bit from [Dr C], I'm not going to repeat it, about the next entries. There are a series of medications or interventions that were attempted. Do you recall that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: At one point we were told that, round about 01.01, [Baby E]'s heart recovered.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Do you remember [Baby E]'s parents being present by this stage?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Vaguely. But I can't remember exactly when they arrived. I know they were there for some...
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Tell us, please, then from your own recollection what, if anything, you can remember from the attempts to resuscitate [Baby E].
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So one thing I remember, and it's alluded to there, is the likely arterial -- is that I cannulated him during the resuscitation to get a blood gas. The blood supply was incredibly poor. This was when he had a heart rate.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Normally, you'd expect things to bleed quite freely once your blood pressure is going and if you hit an artery then, as you've seen on the telly, things tend to bleed quite a lot quicker, and where I'd put the cannula, it bled like it was a vein, but during the CPR the blood started to shoot quite quickly out. So it suggested that the blood -- at that point his blood supply, the amount of blood left in his body was low.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: I remember through the CPR there being quite a lot of significant blood coming through the -- although the amount wasn't particularly -- it wasn't very nice.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So just pausing there. You fitted a cannula --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: -- to what you believed was an artery?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Believed was a vein at the time, but during the process of the CPR was more evident to be an artery. So that -the fact that that wasn't squirting blood suggested that there wasn't a huge amount of blood that was flowing.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: It also is important because the blood gas that you do, it's much better if it's a -- we want it to be an arterial sample, not a sample from a vein.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So if it's very poor from an arterial sample, that's much more reliable of an indication of what's happening than from a vein.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So that's why that's mentioned there and has had an impact on why we've discontinued.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. As we're squeezing on the chest, there's blood coming out of the -- around the nose and mouth during that resuscitation.

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: For the heart rate to come back?
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: From that period of time, yes, once you're kind of going for 10, 15 minutes. The longer it happens, the less likely it is to come back. Ten, 15 minutes is -- I wouldn't personally want to go on longer than 20 minutes. blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Clearly, attempts then continued, given --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: When the heart rate comes above 60, you would stop doing the chest compressions. Now this is around 90 to 100, you would stop doing the chest compressions, but help -- still continue to breathe for him.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: We can see that then, sadly --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Things have started to drop again --
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: -- (overspeaking) heart rate began to fall and eventually CPR was stopped?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No. No. I've seen it in a teenager. I have never seen this in a baby to this extent.

blocks.text: Does that include the period since events in --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't remember from my recollection. From the notes I've obviously spoken -- I would have then spoken to the parents, but I don't remember whether they were there exactly when I arrived.

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: There's PT and there's -- don't ask me what APTT stands for.

blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: All right. Let's hope so. Thank you very much. See you tomorrow at 10.30, please.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the absence of the jury)

Mr Myers, I didn't ask you this in the presence of the jury, but just for my benefit, is it the defence case that there was no discolouration of the kind described in its various forms by the witnesses of [Baby E] or not?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No, it's the -- what we say is the adding of details from the point at which they're first observed and then the merging of them into a composite that suggests there is one kind of discolouration that identified an air embolus and applies across the various witnesses, to which we take exception. We haven't challenged, for instance, that there was a purple discolouration.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Well, exactly. That's why I didn't want to sort of jump in and create a problem by doing that.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So a positive case is not going to be put forward that there was no such discolouration?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No, there's not. It's the way in which the accounts develop over time, we say.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I understand that.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: And the way in which it's being said there is a discolouration that's somehow characteristic. That is the point to which we take exception.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: That's all right, because obviously on the evidence in the case of [Baby E], Ms Letby was present throughout all this, so had the opportunity to see it because she was involved in it all.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: And your Lordship will see what she says about that in fact. We'll see there's no issue taken to a discolouration, it's the way it's being dealt with.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Exactly. I understand that. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS
